title: Cache-aside: the first read pays for the miss, the next ones are hits
caption: The application owns the logic: look in the cache, fall back to the database, then fill the cache with a TTL.

messages.label: GET user:42
messages.note: First request for this user: the cache has never seen the key.

messages.label: SELECT … WHERE id = 42
messages.note: Only now does the database do any work: about 20 ms.

messages.label: SET user:42 row EX 300
messages.note: Store the copy with a 5-minute TTL so a missed invalidation can't live forever.

messages.label: GET user:42 (next request)
messages.note: Every later read within the TTL is a ~0.5 ms hit, and the database is untouched.

scenarios.name: Cache node dies
scenarios.summary: Every read becomes a miss at once, and a database sized for the miss rate gets the full read rate: the herd can take it down too.

messages.label: GET user:42
messages.note: The cache node has crashed: the GET times out.

messages.label: SELECT … WHERE id = 42
messages.note: The app falls back to the database, and so does every other request on every server.

messages.label: timeout (overloaded)
messages.note: With a 95% hit rate the database normally sees 5% of reads; now it sees 100%, twenty times its load.

messages.label: short timeout + breaker
messages.note: Mitigation: fail fast on the cache, limit DB concurrency, serve a fallback, and run cache replicas so one node's loss isn't total.

scenarios.name: Key that doesn't exist
scenarios.summary: A miss that the database also misses caches nothing, so lookups for absent keys hit the database every time. Cache the 'not found' too.

messages.label: GET user:999999
messages.note: A scraper (or a bug) asks for ids that don't exist.

messages.label: SELECT … WHERE id = 999999
messages.note: The row isn't there either, so there is nothing to cache and the next request repeats the query.

messages.label: SET user:999999 NONE EX 60
messages.note: Fix: cache a short-lived 'not found' marker, or check a Bloom filter of existing ids first.

scenarios.name: Alternative: read-through
scenarios.summary: The cache loads misses itself, so the app only ever talks to the cache. Simpler callers, but the cache layer must know how to query the database.
scenarios.caption: Read-through moves the miss handling from the application into the cache (or a cache library).

messages.label: GET user:42
messages.note: The app asks the cache and nothing else.

messages.label: load user:42
messages.note: On a miss the cache (or its loader library) queries the database itself.

messages.label: row (stored with TTL)
messages.note: The cache stores the copy and answers. Same latency as cache-aside; the logic just lives in one place.
